title: Americans Want Better Brain Health but Few Know Where to Start, Survey Finds
excerpt: New Alzheimer's Association report reveals 88% of adults consider brain health a top priority but only 9% know how to maintain it
body:
• A survey of 3,800+ US adults 40 and older found 88% consider maintaining brain health as they age very important, yet only 9% say they know a lot about how to do it
  • An estimated 7.4 million Americans aged 65 and older are living with Alzheimer's disease, with deaths more than doubling since 2000
  • Key protective habits — sleep, diet, exercise and mental stimulation — are widely recognized but poorly practiced: only 50% get seven hours of sleep and 39% eat a healthy diet regularly
  • Experts say midlife is the critical window to start building habits that support cognitive longevity

Nearly nine in ten Americans consider brain health a top priority as they age, rating it at least as important as physical health. But a sweeping gap between awareness and action persists, according to the 2026 Alzheimer's Disease Facts and Figures report released by the Alzheimer's Association.

The survey of more than 3,800 US adults aged 40 and older found that 99% consider maintaining brain health at least as important as physical health, yet only 9% said they know a lot about how to actually protect it. More than two-thirds worry about developing Alzheimer's disease or other forms of dementia.

The Knowledge Gap

While most Americans surveyed (99%) believe lifestyle behaviors play a role in brain health, fewer than half strongly connected those behaviors to a reduced risk of Alzheimer's or dementia. That disconnect is striking given decades of research showing that good nutrition, regular exercise, quality sleep and mental stimulation can significantly support cognitive function.

"Americans care deeply about their brain health and say that midlife is the key time to start taking steps to support it. But many don't know where to start and are looking for clear guidance on actions they can take."

— Heather Snyder, SVP Medical & Scientific Relations, Alzheimer's Association

When asked about specific habits that support brain health, respondents most frequently cited protecting against head injury (82%), not smoking (72%), managing stress (71%) and treating depression (71%). These are all valid, but the survey revealed that people were less likely to connect everyday lifestyle choices — like sleep and diet — to brain protection.

Practice Trails Awareness

Even among those who recognize the importance of brain-healthy habits, follow-through is inconsistent. Only half of those surveyed reported getting at least seven hours of sleep on most nights. Just 39% said they regularly eat a healthy, balanced diet. Physical activity rates were similarly modest.

These numbers matter because a growing body of research, including a 2026 study in the journal Neurology, has shown that people who engage in lifelong cognitive enrichment — from reading and learning new skills to maintaining social connections — have onset of Alzheimer's delayed by as much as five years compared to those with the lowest levels of mental stimulation.

The Scale of the Crisis

The report estimates that 7.4 million Americans aged 65 and older are currently living with clinical Alzheimer's dementia. Between 2000 and 2024, the number of US deaths attributed to Alzheimer's more than doubled, underscoring both the disease's growing prevalence and the urgency of prevention efforts.

Separate research from the University of Birmingham has found that maintaining good overall brain health can help reduce the impact of early Alzheimer's-related changes on cognitive function, even when biomarkers for the disease are already present.

What You Can Do

Experts say midlife — roughly ages 40 to 65 — is the critical window for building brain-protective habits. The evidence points to several actionable steps: regular physical activity (at least 150 minutes per week), a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables and whole grains, consistent quality sleep of seven to nine hours, ongoing mental stimulation through learning or social engagement, and proactive management of conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes.

While there is no guaranteed way to prevent Alzheimer's, the research consensus is clear: it is never too early, or too late, to start making choices that support cognitive health.
